aimTitle: Cyber security threats, system vulnerabilities and security protection methods
aimShort: Internal and external threats, vulnerabilities, legislation, protection measures
board: Pearson BTEC Level 3 National Extended Certificate in IT (AAQ)
assessment: Externally assessed written exam (set + marked by Pearson).

topics.name: Cyber security threats
Internal threats: employee sabotage (deliberate/accidental); accidental or deliberate damage; weak cyber security measures and unsafe practices; accidental loss or disclosure of data/credentials

External threats: malware (viruses, spyware, adware, ransomware, bots); hacking (DoS/DDoS, browser hijack, cyberwarfare, data theft/tampering); sabotage; social engineering (phishing, vishing, smishing, whaling, spear phishing, DNS spoofing, pretexting); physical security (tailgating, shoulder surfing, theft)
Impact of a credible threat: operational loss, financial loss, reputational loss, intellectual property loss
Threat landscape updates: NCSC UK, NIST USA, OWASP Top 10
System vulnerabilities
Vulnerabilities of systems: network (firewall ports), organisational (permissions, password policy/management), software, OS/GUI/CLI, mobile devices, physical, people/process, cloud computing and IoT
Sources of vulnerability information: manufacturer
Attack vectors: wireless (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, satellite, IR, NFC, RFID), internet connection, internal network access devices
Vulnerability assessment tools: port scanner, network mapper, registry checker, website vulnerability scanner, vulnerability detection software, user vulnerability assessment
Independent third-party review: due diligence, third-party certification
Penetration testing: finding weak spots, checking against known vulnerabilities, producing reports
Passive risk management measures: risk transfer, risk avoidance, risk acceptance
Legal responsibilities
Current legislation: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Computer Misuse Act 1990
Areas legislation applies to: data protection in storage and transfer, privacy/PII, unauthorised access to computers and data
Legal responsibilities: GDPR principles, legal reasons for processing, personal rights; Computer Misuse Act responsibilities
Software and hardware security measures
Physical security; data storage/backup/recovery; antivirus; firewalls; authentication; access controls (DAC, RBAC); trusted computing; finding lost/stolen devices; device-based security
Encryption: storage encryption, communications encryption (symmetric AES, asymmetric RSA/Diffie-Hellman, TOR, VPN, HTTPS, E2EE)
WLAN protection: MAC filtering, SSID hiding, WPA2/3, WPS, wireless vulnerabilities and mitigation
Security by design: expect attacks, fewest privileges, no reliance on secrecy, ISO 27000 compliance

examQuestions.question: State one category of external threat to an organisation's systems.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for any valid category of external threat.
points: Malicious software / malware (1)
Hacking (1)
Sabotage (1)
Social engineering (1)
Physical security (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any of the five external-threat categories.

examQuestions.question: Identify the type of malware that encrypts a victim's files and demands a payment to restore access.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct term.
points: Ransomware (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An IT services company has discovered that several workstations have been infected with software that encrypts all files and demands payment.
examQuestions.question: Describe the type of malware that has infected the workstations.

points: Ransomware â€” malware that encrypts the victim's files/data (1)
The attacker demands a ransom payment (usually cryptocurrency) in exchange for the decryption key (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any two relevant points. Do not accept: virus (too generic).

examQuestions.scenario: A financial services company's security team detected that an attacker had installed software that records every keystroke made by employees on the finance systems.
examQuestions.question: Explain how this type of malware operates and the risks it poses to the organisation.

points: This is a keylogger â€” malware that secretly records every keystroke typed by the user (1)
It can capture usernames, passwords, bank account details and other sensitive information (1)
Risk: financial fraud, data breach leading to GDPR fines, reputational damage, loss of customer trust (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept other valid risks linked to the scenario.

examQuestions.question: State one difference between a virus and a worm.

points: A virus requires user interaction (opening a file) to spread, whereas a worm can self-replicate and spread automatically across networks without user action (1)

examQuestions.question: Identify the social engineering technique where an attacker sends fraudulent emails pretending to be a trusted organisation to trick recipients into revealing sensitive information.

points: Phishing (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A senior executive at an IT services company received an email that appeared to be from the CEO, urgently requesting a large bank transfer. The email address was subtly different from the CEO's real email.
examQuestions.question: Describe the type of social engineering attack being used.

points: Whaling / spear phishing â€” a targeted phishing attack aimed at senior executives (1)
The attacker impersonates a high-level authority figure (CEO) to pressure the victim into taking urgent action without verification (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept spear phishing with explanation. Do not accept: phishing (too generic without targeting context).

examQuestions.question: State what is meant by 'tailgating' in the context of physical security.

points: Tailgating is when an unauthorised person follows an authorised person through a secured door/entry point without using their own credentials/authentication (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An e-commerce website for a retail business was inaccessible for three hours after being flooded with millions of fake requests from compromised devices across the world.
examQuestions.question: Explain the type of attack that occurred and the impact on the business.

points: This is a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack â€” multiple compromised devices (botnet) flood the server with traffic (1)
The server becomes overwhelmed and cannot respond to legitimate customer requests (1)
Impact: loss of sales revenue during downtime, customer frustration and potential loss of future business (1)
Reputational damage â€” customers may perceive the business as unreliable or insecure and switch to competitors (1)

examQuestions.question: Identify the type of network attack where an attacker secretly intercepts and potentially alters communication between two parties who believe they are directly communicating with each other.

points: Man-in-the-Middle / MITM attack (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A healthcare organisation is still running Windows 7 on several workstations that handle patient data.
examQuestions.question: Explain the security risks of continuing to use unsupported operating systems.

points: End-of-life operating systems no longer receive security patches/updates from the vendor (1)
Any newly discovered vulnerabilities remain permanently exploitable as they will never be fixed (1)
This creates a significant risk of data breaches, which for patient data could result in GDPR fines of up to Â£17.5 million and severe reputational damage (1)

examQuestions.question: Identify the term for a software vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor and for which no patch exists.

points: Zero-day vulnerability / zero-day exploit (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe two poor password practices that create vulnerabilities in an organisation.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark each for two valid practices described.
points: Using weak/short passwords that are easily guessed or cracked by brute force (1)
Reusing the same password across multiple systems â€” if one system is compromised, all accounts become vulnerable (1)
Writing passwords down on sticky notes near the workstation â€” visible to passers-by (1)
Sharing passwords with colleagues â€” no accountability for actions taken (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A retail business suffered a data breach exposing 50,000 customers' personal data including names, email addresses, and payment card details.
examQuestions.question: Explain the legal implications under UK GDPR for the organisation.

points: Under UK GDPR, the organisation has a legal obligation to protect personal data with appropriate technical and organisational measures (1)
The organisation must notify the ICO (Information Commissioner's Office) within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach (1)
They must also notify affected individuals without undue delay if the breach poses a high risk to their rights and freedoms (1)
Maximum penalty: fine of up to Â£17.5 million or 4% of annual global turnover, whichever is higher (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe the purpose of an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) in an organisation.

points: An AUP is a document that sets out the rules and guidelines for how employees may use the organisation's IT systems and network (1)
It covers permitted activities, prohibited behaviour (e.g. accessing inappropriate websites), data handling requirements, and consequences for breaching the policy (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — physical
examQuestions.question: Identify one biometric method used for physical access control to secure areas.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for any valid biometric method.
points: Fingerprint recognition / fingerprint scanner (1)
Iris / retina scanning (1)
Facial recognition (1)
Voice recognition (1)
Hand geometry (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any one valid biometric method. Do not accept: smart card or PIN (not biometric).

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — antivirus
examQuestions.question: Explain the difference between signature-based detection and heuristic analysis in antivirus software.

points: Signature-based detection compares files against a database of known malware signatures/patterns â€” it can only detect previously identified threats (1)
Heuristic analysis examines the behaviour and characteristics of files to identify potentially malicious code even if no signature exists (1)

Heuristic analysis can detect new/unknown malware (zero-day threats), but may produce false positives, while signature-based is more reliable for known threats but ineffective against new variants (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — firewalls
examQuestions.question: Describe the function of a firewall in protecting a network.

points: A firewall monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules (1)
It acts as a barrier between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks, blocking unauthorised access while permitting legitimate communication (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — authentication
examQuestions.scenario: A financial services company is implementing Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for all employee access to sensitive systems.
examQuestions.question: Explain the three categories of authentication factors used in MFA and why using multiple factors improves security.

points: Something you know â€” e.g. password, PIN, security question answer (1)
Something you have â€” e.g. smartphone (for authenticator app), security token, smart card (1)
Something you are â€” e.g. fingerprint, facial recognition, iris scan (biometrics) (1)
Using multiple factors means that even if an attacker obtains one factor (e.g. steals password), they still cannot access the system without the other factor(s) â€” defence in depth (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — access controls
examQuestions.question: Describe the principle of 'least privilege' in access control.

points: Users are granted only the minimum level of access/permissions necessary to perform their job role (1)
This limits the potential damage from compromised accounts, accidental changes, or insider threats â€” an attacker who gains access to a user account can only access what that user can access (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.

points: Symmetric encryption uses the same key for both encryption and decryption â€” it is fast and efficient for bulk data (1)
Asymmetric encryption uses a key pair: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption â€” it is more secure for key exchange but slower (1)
In practice, asymmetric encryption (e.g. RSA) is often used to securely exchange a symmetric session key, which is then used for the actual data transfer (e.g. in TLS/HTTPS) (1)

examQuestions.question: State the purpose of a digital certificate in secure web communications (HTTPS).

points: A digital certificate verifies the identity/authenticity of a website/server, issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA), to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks and phishing (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain how a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack poses a greater risk to an organisation than a single-source denial of service (DoS) attack.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award up to four marks for a point and linked expansion.
points: A DDoS attack uses many compromised devices (a botnet) to flood the target simultaneously (1)
whereas a DoS attack comes from a single source (1)
DDoS is harder to block because traffic comes from many IP addresses (1)
so the target is overwhelmed for longer, denying service to more legitimate users (1)

examQuestions.question: State two examples of internal threats to an organisation.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark per correct example, up to two marks.
points: Employee sabotage, deliberate or accidental (1)
Accidental or deliberate damage (fire, flood, power loss) (1)
Weak cyber security measures and unsafe practices (1)
Accidental loss or disclosure of data/credentials (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An IT services company discovered that several servers have been recruited into a botnet and are being used to send spam emails.
examQuestions.question: Describe what a botnet is and how the servers may have become compromised.

points: A botnet is a network of compromised devices controlled remotely by an attacker (botmaster) via command-and-control (C2) servers (1)
Devices become part of a botnet when infected with malware — typically through phishing emails, drive-by downloads, or exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities (1)
Once compromised, the attacker can use the devices for DDoS attacks, spam distribution, cryptocurrency mining, or data theft without the owner's knowledge (1)

examQuestions.question: Compare a virus and a worm, explaining how each spreads and the relative threat they pose to an organisation's network.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award up to four marks — must include comparison.
points: A virus attaches itself to legitimate files and requires user action (opening a file, running a program) to activate and spread (1)
A worm self-replicates and spreads automatically across networks by exploiting vulnerabilities — no user interaction required (1)
Worms pose a greater threat to network infrastructure because they can spread rapidly without human intervention, potentially infecting hundreds of systems in minutes (1)
However, viruses can be more targeted and harder to detect initially since they hide within legitimate files (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An employee at a financial services company received a phone call from someone claiming to be from the IT department, asking for their login credentials to 'fix a server issue'.
examQuestions.question: Explain the type of social engineering attack being used and recommend two measures the company should implement to prevent such attacks.

points: This is vishing (voice phishing) — the attacker impersonates a trusted internal department (IT) to extract credentials (1)
Measure 1: Implement a policy that IT will NEVER ask for passwords over the phone — all credential resets must go through an approved self-service portal (1)
Measure 2: Regular security awareness training including simulated vishing exercises so employees learn to recognise and report suspicious calls (1)
Additional: Implement MFA so that even if credentials are compromised via vishing, the attacker cannot access systems without the second factor (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe two physical social engineering techniques and how they bypass security controls.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for each technique described.
points: Tailgating: following an authorised person through a secure door without using own credentials — bypasses access control systems entirely (1)
Shoulder surfing: watching someone type their password or view sensitive data on screen — bypasses technical authentication controls (1)
Baiting: leaving infected USB drives in public areas hoping someone picks them up and plugs them in — bypasses network perimeter defences (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An e-commerce website for a retail business was inaccessible for four hours due to a DDoS attack during a major sale event.
examQuestions.question: Explain the impact of the DDoS attack on the business, including financial and non-financial consequences.

points: Direct financial loss: the business lost four hours of sales during a peak sale period — potentially thousands of pounds in lost revenue (1)
Reputational damage: customers unable to access the site may lose trust and switch to competitors — long-term loss of customer loyalty (1)
Operational costs: IT staff must work to mitigate the attack, potentially requiring expensive DDoS mitigation services (1)
Customer service impact: increased complaints and support tickets, further straining resources after the attack (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An employee at a healthcare organisation accessed patient records without authorisation out of curiosity. They did not modify or share the data.
examQuestions.question: Explain which UK legislation has been breached and the potential consequences.

points: This breaches Section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 — unauthorised access to computer material (1)
Even though no data was modified or shared, simply accessing the system without authorisation is an offence — maximum 2 years imprisonment (1)
This also breaches UK GDPR principles — personal data must be processed lawfully and only for specified purposes (1)
Consequences: criminal prosecution under CMA, potential GDPR fine for the organisation, disciplinary action including dismissal, and mandatory reporting to the ICO (1)

examQuestions.question: State two rights that individuals have under UK GDPR.

points: Right of access — individuals can request a copy of all personal data held about them (Subject Access Request) (1)
Right to erasure ('right to be forgotten') — individuals can request deletion of their personal data (1)
Right to data portability — receive personal data in a machine-readable format (1)
Right to object — opt out of direct marketing and automated decision-making (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A financial services company needs to protect customer data both when stored on their servers and when transmitted over the internet for online banking.
examQuestions.question: Explain the encryption methods that should be used for data at rest and data in transit, and why both are necessary.

points: Data at rest (stored on servers): use symmetric encryption such as AES-256 for disk/database encryption — fast and efficient for large volumes of stored data (1)
Data in transit (online banking): use TLS/HTTPS which employs asymmetric encryption (RSA) to exchange a symmetric session key — secures the connection between browser and server (1)

Both are necessary because protecting only data at rest leaves data vulnerable during transmission (MITM attacks), while protecting only data in transit leaves stored data vulnerable to physical theft or server breach (1)
This is an example of defence in depth — multiple layers of encryption ensure that if one layer is compromised, data remains protected by the other (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — firewalls
examQuestions.question: Describe how a stateful inspection firewall differs from a packet filtering firewall.

points: Packet filtering inspects each packet in isolation — only checks headers (IP, port) against static rules without context (1)
Stateful inspection maintains a state table tracking active connections — it understands whether a packet is part of an established connection or a new request (1)
Stateful inspection is more secure because it can detect and block packets that are spoofed or out of sequence, whereas packet filtering might allow them if they match header rules (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — access controls
examQuestions.scenario: A large organisation has employees across HR, Finance, IT, and Sales departments who all need access to different systems.
examQuestions.question: Explain how Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) would be implemented and why it is more manageable than Discretionary Access Control (DAC) for this organisation.

points: RBAC assigns permissions to roles (HR role, Finance role, etc.) rather than to individual users — users are assigned to roles based on their job function (1)
When a new employee joins, they are simply assigned the appropriate role and automatically receive all necessary permissions — no individual configuration needed (1)
RBAC is more manageable at scale because changing permissions for a role automatically applies to all users in that role — with DAC, each user's permissions must be set individually (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — authentication
examQuestions.scenario: A healthcare organisation is considering implementing Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for all staff accessing patient record systems. Some staff have raised concerns about convenience.
examQuestions.question: Evaluate the benefits and drawbacks of implementing MFA for the healthcare organisation.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award up to six marks — must include balanced evaluation.
points: Benefit: MFA significantly reduces the risk of unauthorised access — even if a password is stolen (phishing, shoulder surfing), the attacker cannot access the system without the second factor (1)
Benefit: For healthcare data, this is critical — patient records are highly sensitive and a breach would violate GDPR, potentially resulting in fines up to £17.5 million (1)
Benefit: MFA can use biometrics (fingerprint) which is fast and convenient for clinical staff who need quick access — no typing required (1)
Drawback: Staff may resist the change — needing a phone/token for every login adds steps and can be perceived as inconvenient, especially in fast-paced clinical environments (1)
Drawback: Lost or forgotten tokens/phones can lock staff out of systems, potentially delaying patient care — requires a backup authentication process (1)

Overall judgement: Despite convenience concerns, the security benefits outweigh the drawbacks given the sensitivity of healthcare data and regulatory requirements — the organisation should implement MFA with biometric options and a clear backup process (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe what is meant by a supply chain vulnerability in cybersecurity.

points: A supply chain vulnerability occurs when a third-party vendor, supplier, or partner has access to an organisation's systems or data — their security weaknesses become your security weaknesses (1)
If the vendor is compromised, attackers can use that access to infiltrate the target organisation — the organisation is only as secure as its weakest supplier (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe how phishing is used to obtain secure information by deception.

points: Fraudulent emails are sent that appear to come from a trusted organisation (1)
they trick the recipient into clicking a malicious link or opening an attachment (1)
the recipient then reveals credentials or the link installs malware (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain how a denial of service (DoS) attack is carried out.

points: The attacker sends a large number of requests/pings/packets to a server or gateway (1)
so the server/system is overwhelmed (1)
it cannot service legitimate requests (1)
causing it to slow, stop or crash, denying normal service (1)

examQuestions.topic: A1.3 Impact of a credible threat
examQuestions.question: Explain two types of loss an organisation may suffer following a credible cyber security threat.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award up to two marks per explained loss.
points: Operational loss — reduced manufacturing output, service availability or data availability (2)
Financial loss — loss of profits, cash-flow problems, compensation payments, fines or legal fees (2)
Reputational loss — loss of trust, poor reviews, reduced reputation scores (2)
Intellectual property loss — loss of designs, strategy or trade secrets (2)

examQuestions.scenario: A logistics firm found that a worm spread across its LAN without any users opening attachments.
examQuestions.question: Explain how a worm differs from a virus and why it spreads so rapidly.

points: A worm self-replicates and propagates automatically across networks (1)
A virus requires a host file and user action (opening or running it) to spread (1)
A worm spreads automatically by exploiting vulnerabilities or network shares, needing no human interaction (1)
This automatic propagation lets it infect many devices rapidly, making containment harder (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A marketing firm computers show many pop-up adverts and run slowly, but no files appear encrypted.
examQuestions.question: Explain why these symptoms are consistent with adware rather than ransomware.

points: Adware displays persistent adverts and slows systems without encrypting data (1)
Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment - no such demand or encryption has occurred (1)
Adware may also track browsing and gather data, a privacy and confidentiality risk (1)
Even though less destructive, adware can be a gateway for more serious malware and should be removed (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A finance employee received an email appearing to be from the CEO urgently requesting a large transfer to a new supplier account.
examQuestions.question: Explain why this is a whaling attack and how it exploits human trust.

points: Whaling is spear-phishing that targets a senior figure (here impersonating the CEO) (1)
Urgency and apparent authority pressure the victim to act quickly without verification (1)
It exploits the human tendency to trust messages from a recognised senior colleague (1)
It bypasses technical controls, so awareness training and a verification procedure are key defences (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A caller claimed to be from IT helpdesk and asked an employee to reveal their password.
examQuestions.question: Explain how vishing works and why it can bypass email-based protections.

points: Vishing (voice phishing) uses phone calls to trick victims into revealing sensitive information (1)
Attackers impersonate a trusted contact, such as IT support, to appear legitimate (1)
It bypasses email filters because no email is involved, so staff must verify via a different channel (1)

examQuestions.question: State two examples of baiting attacks.

points: Leaving an infected USB drive where someone will plug it in (1)
Offering a free download or gift that installs malware when accessed (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any two valid baiting examples.

examQuestions.scenario: An attacker observes an employee typing their password and later follows them through a secure door.
examQuestions.question: Explain how shoulder surfing and tailgating compromise physical security.

points: Shoulder surfing is secretly observing a user entering credentials or viewing sensitive data over their shoulder (1)
Tailgating is following an authorised person through a secure door without using your own credentials (1)
Both bypass technical access controls and rely on human behaviour, so privacy screens and challenge policies help mitigate them (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An online shop is repeatedly knocked offline during sales by huge volumes of traffic from thousands of different IP addresses.
examQuestions.question: Explain why this is a DDoS attack and the impact it has on the business.

points: A DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) attack floods a target with traffic from many compromised devices (a botnet), overwhelming it (1)
The flood exhausts resources so legitimate customers cannot access the site (1)
This causes lost sales and revenue during peak periods such as sales events (1)
It also damages reputation and customer trust, and may require costly mitigation services (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe three physical threats to an organisation systems.

points: Theft of devices or media containing sensitive data (1)
Sabotage or intentional damage by a disgruntled individual (1)
Natural disasters, hardware failure or power loss (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A company runs an operating system that no longer receives security updates.
examQuestions.question: Explain why running unsupported (end-of-life) software increases cyber risk.

points: End-of-life software no longer receives security patches, so known vulnerabilities remain open (1)
Attackers can exploit known, documented flaws that will never be fixed (1)
This makes the organisation a lower-effort, more attractive target (1)
The organisation should upgrade, isolate or apply compensating controls to reduce exposure (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe what is meant by a zero-day vulnerability.

points: A vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor and has no patch at the time it is exploited (1)
It is dangerous because there is no fix and it can be exploited before being discovered (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An auditor found an open port offering an unencrypted service access to the internet.
examQuestions.question: Explain why an unnecessarily open network port is a security risk and how to reduce it.

points: An open port exposes a service to the internet, increasing the attack surface (1)
If the service has vulnerabilities or weak credentials, an attacker can gain access (1)
Close unused ports, restrict access by firewall rules, and secure or encrypt any service that is needed (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe what a rogue access point is.

points: An unauthorised wireless access point connected to the network, often to bypass controls (1)
It can let attackers intercept traffic or gain network access; wireless detection helps (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An attacker phished one employee who reused the same password across many systems, taking over several accounts.
examQuestions.question: Explain how poor password practices create a vulnerability and how policies can reduce it.

points: Password reuse means one compromised password grants access to many accounts (1)
Weak or easily guessed passwords can be cracked by brute-force or dictionary attacks (1)
Training staff to use unique, strong passwords and a password manager helps (1)
Adding MFA and checking against breach databases provides protection even if a password is compromised (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A software vendor used by the company was breached, exposing the company.
examQuestions.question: Explain how a supply-chain partner can increase an organisation attack surface.

points: A vendor often has privileged access to the organisation systems or data (1)
If the vendor is compromised, attackers can use that trusted access to reach the organisation (1)
Organisations should vet suppliers, limit their access, and monitor third-party activity (1)

examQuestions.scenario: An employee accessed patient records without authorisation out of curiosity, without sharing them.
examQuestions.question: Explain which UK legislation is breached and the potential consequences.

points: Unauthorised access breaches Section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (1)
Even without modifying data, simply accessing a system without authorisation is an offence (1)
It also breaches the UK GDPR / Data Protection Act principle of lawful, least-authorisation processing of personal data (1)
Consequences can include criminal prosecution, GDPR fines for the organisation, disciplinary action, and reporting to the ICO (1)

examQuestions.question: State two rights an individual has under UK GDPR.

points: Right of access - to obtain a copy of personal data held about them (subject access request) (1)
Right to erasure (right to be forgotten) - to request deletion of their data (1)
Also accept: right to portability, right to object, right to rectification.
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award one mark per right, up to two.

examQuestions.scenario: An organisation stores customer records and is reviewing its legal obligations.
examQuestions.question: Explain one legal responsibility an organisation has under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

points: Process personal data lawfully, fairly and transparently (1)
Keep data accurate and only for the stated purpose, storing the minimum amount for the minimum time (1)
Maintain confidentiality and integrity by applying appropriate technical and organisational security measures (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any GDPR principle or personal right (access, erasure, rectification, objection, portability).

examQuestions.scenario: A company is designing a new networked system and wants to build security in from the start.
examQuestions.question: Explain one principle of security by design.

points: Expect attacks to happen and plan for them rather than assuming the system is safe (1)
Design the system to run on 'fewest privileges' so users/applications have only the access they need (1)
Avoid reliance on secrecy/obscurity, and comply with information security standards such as ISO 27000 (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any security-by-design principle (expect attacks, fewest privileges, no reliance on secrecy, ISO 27000 compliance).

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — physical
examQuestions.question: Describe three physical security controls for protecting a server room.

points: Biometric or PIN access control to restrict who can enter (1)
CCTV to monitor and deter unauthorised activity (1)
Locks, alarms and protected cabling to provide additional layers of protection (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — backup/recovery
examQuestions.scenario: A firm lost a days worth of data when a server failed because its backups were outdated.
examQuestions.question: Explain the difference between full, differential and incremental backups and the trade-offs.

points: A full backup copies all data, providing a complete baseline but is the slowest to create (1)
A differential backup stores all changes since the last full backup (1)
An incremental backup stores changes since the last backup of any type, being faster to make but requiring all previous ones to restore (1)
Trade-off: full backups restore fastest but are slow to create; incremental backups are fast to create but slower and more complex to restore (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — antivirus
examQuestions.scenario: A new malware variant avoided detection because it had no matching signature.
examQuestions.question: Explain the difference between signature-based and heuristic detection and why new malware may evade signature detection.

points: Signature-based detection matches known malware patterns, so it misses new or unknown malware (1)
Heuristic analysis looks for suspicious behaviour or characteristics to catch unknown variants (1)
A new variant with no matching signature bypasses signature-based detection until a signature is created (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — firewalls
examQuestions.question: Describe how a stateful inspection firewall differs from a packet-filtering firewall.

points: Packet filtering inspects each packet header against static rules in isolation (1)
Stateful inspection tracks the state of active connections and understands their context (1)
Stateful inspection can block packets that appear to be part of an established connection but are actually unauthorised (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — authentication
examQuestions.scenario: A healthcare organisation is considering requiring staff to use two authentication factors.
examQuestions.question: Explain how multi-factor authentication (MFA) improves security.

points: MFA requires evidence from two or more different categories such as something you know, have, or are (1)
Even if a password is stolen, the attacker still needs the other factor to authenticate (1)
This significantly reduces the impact of phishing, password reuse and credential theft (1)
Examples include a password combined with a one-time code or a fingerprint (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — access controls
examQuestions.scenario: A large organisation has employees across HR, Finance and Sales who need different access levels.
examQuestions.question: Explain how Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) is more manageable than Discretionary Access Control (DAC) at scale.

points: RBAC assigns permissions to roles rather than to each individual user (1)
Users are added to a role and automatically gain its permissions (1)
RBAC is more manageable because changing a role applies to all its members, whereas DAC requires setting rights per user (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A coffee shop offers open Wi-Fi and a customer later found their account drained.
examQuestions.question: Explain the risks of using open, unencrypted Wi-Fi and how to reduce them.

points: Open Wi-Fi is unencrypted, so traffic can be intercepted and sniffed (1)
A malicious evil-twin hotspot can impersonate the legitimate access point (1)
This can expose credentials and session data (1)
Use HTTPS or a VPN, avoid sensitive transactions on public Wi-Fi, and disable automatic joining of unknown networks (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A finance firm must protect data stored on servers and data sent over the internet.
examQuestions.question: Explain the encryption methods used for data at rest and data in transit, and why both are needed.

points: Data at rest is protected with symmetric encryption such as AES for disks and databases (1)
Data in transit is protected with TLS/HTTPS, which uses asymmetric encryption to exchange a symmetric session key (1)
Both are needed because an attacker could otherwise target either stored or transmitted data (1)
Using both is an example of defence in depth (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.

points: Symmetric encryption uses a single shared key for both encryption and decryption (1)
Asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair, where one key encrypts and the other decrypts (1)
Symmetric is faster but requires secure key exchange; asymmetric solves key distribution but is slower (1)

examQuestions.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — device-based security
examQuestions.question: Describe two measures to secure a lost or stolen mobile device.

points: Remote wipe to erase data if the device is lost or stolen (1)
Screen lock (PIN or biometric) to prevent casual access (1)
Device encryption and GPS tracking to protect data and help locate the device (1)

examQuestions.scenario: A development team plans a new web application that will store sensitive data.
examQuestions.question: Explain why threat modelling should be completed before deployment.

points: Threat modelling identifies potential threats and attack vectors early in development (1)
It allows security controls to be built in from the start rather than added later (1)
This reduces overall risk and the cost of fixing vulnerabilities later (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe the principle of least privilege.

points: Users and processes are given only the minimum access needed to do their job (1)
This limits the damage a compromised account can do (1)

flashcards.front: What are the four categories of internal threat to an organisation?
flashcards.back:
1. Employee sabotage, deliberate and accidental (theft/loss of equipment, data or software; use of unauthorised software)
2. Accidental or deliberate damage (fire, flood, power loss, terrorism)
3. Weak cyber security measures and unsafe practices (poor equipment security, no visitor vetting, visiting untrustworthy websites)
4. Accidental loss or disclosure of data/credentials (negligence, poor training, weak security culture)

flashcards.front: Name the six main types of malware.
flashcards.back:
1. Virus — attaches to files, needs user action to spread
2. Worm — self-replicates across networks automatically
3. Trojan — disguises as legitimate software
4. Ransomware — encrypts files, demands payment
5. Spyware — secretly monitors user activity
6. Rootkit — hides its presence, gives attacker persistent control

flashcards.front: What is the difference between phishing, spear phishing, and whaling?
flashcards.back: Phishing = mass, generic emails pretending to be trusted organisations. Spear phishing = targeted at specific individuals using personal information. Whaling = spear phishing aimed at senior executives (CEOs, CFOs) — higher stakes.

flashcards.front: What are the key provisions of the Computer Misuse Act 1990?
flashcards.back: Section 1: Unauthorised access (up to 2 years). Section 2: Unauthorised access with intent to commit further crime (up to 5 years). Section 3: Unauthorised modification — viruses, deleting files (up to 10 years). Section 3A: Making/supplying hacking tools (up to 2 years).

flashcards.front: What are the maximum penalties under UK GDPR for a data breach?
flashcards.back: Up to £17.5 million OR 4% of the organisation's annual global turnover — whichever is HIGHER. Organisations must also notify the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach.

flashcards.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — firewalls
flashcards.front: What are the different types of firewalls?
flashcards.back:
1. Packet filtering — inspects packet headers, basic
2. Stateful inspection — tracks connection state
3. Application layer / proxy — inspects content at Layer 7
4. Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) — combines traditional firewall with IPS, application awareness, and threat intelligence

flashcards.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — authentication
flashcards.front: What are the three authentication factor categories in MFA?
flashcards.back:
1. Something you KNOW (password, PIN)
2. Something you HAVE (smartphone, token, smart card)
3. Something you ARE (fingerprint, facial recognition, iris scan — biometrics)
4. (Some frameworks add) Somewhere you ARE (geolocation, IP address)
5. (Some frameworks add) Something you DO (typing pattern, signature behaviour)

flashcards.front: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
flashcards.back: Symmetric: Same key encrypts and decrypts (e.g. AES). Fast, suitable for bulk data, but key must be securely shared. Asymmetric: Public key encrypts, private key decrypts (e.g. RSA). Slower but solves the key exchange problem. In practice, asymmetric encryption is used to securely exchange a symmetric session key (hybrid approach in TLS/HTTPS).

flashcards.topic: A4.1 Software and hardware security — backup/recovery
flashcards.back: Keep at least 3 copies of your data, on 2 different types of storage media, with 1 copy stored offsite. This protects against hardware failure, ransomware, fire, flood, and theft simultaneously.

notes.title: Social engineering & malware
passages: [[Phishing]] uses fake emails to trick users into revealing credentials; [[vishing]] uses phone calls and [[smishing]] uses SMS. [[Spear phishing]] targets a [[specific individual]], and [[whaling]] targets senior [[executives]].
[[Ransomware]] [[encrypts]] a victim's files and demands payment. [[Spyware]] secretly [[monitors]] activity. [[Adware]] floods the device with [[advertisements]].
[[DoS/DDoS]] overloads a system with traffic so it becomes [[unavailable]]. A DDoS uses many [[compromised computers]] (a botnet).
The impact of a credible threat is judged as [[operational]], [[financial]], [[reputational]] and [[intellectual-property]] loss.

[[Penetration testing]] is an authorised simulated [[attack]] to find weak spots before attackers do. A [[port scanner]] finds [[open ports]]. Risk can be handled by [[transfer]], [[avoidance]] or [[acceptance]].
